title: The boon beyond compare
hook: the last gift, Satyavan's life given back, and why women still wind thread round a banyan
carry: a vrat offers your fast for another's long life

segments.voice: Yesterday: sat, the good, and satsang, the company of the good. Three gifts from Death, sight, a kingdom and sons, and every one for someone else. Your line was satsang, the company of the good.
screen: `SAT AND SATSANG.` · `THREE GIFTS, ALL GIVEN AWAY.`

segments.voice: Ask once more, says Death. Savitri is still on the road behind Yama, still talking. And this time she asks for something for herself. Let me have sons, she says, sons of my own, born of Satyavan. Yama grants it. So be it. She keeps walking, and keeps speaking about the good. A gift has now been given that can only come true one way. And the noose in Yama's hand is still closed.
screen: `ASK ONCE MORE.` → `SONS, BORN OF SATYAVAN.` → `THE NOOSE STILL CLOSED.`

segments.voice: In the epic this isn't a clever trap. It's a conversation won. Savitri speaks again about the good, how they keep to the truth and hold up the world, and Yama, pleased once more, tells her to ask for something beyond compare. Savitri asks plainly. The gift you gave me can't come true without my husband. Without him I don't want happiness, or heaven, or my own life. Let Satyavan live. And Yama loosens the noose. Satyavan opens his eyes in her lap like a man waking from a long sleep. It's night, he's weak and frightened for his parents, so Savitri ties up her hair, helps him up, carries his axe, and they walk home through the dark. The sage Markandeya, who tells this story to the exiled Pandavas, promises them that Draupadi will save them the same way. Now the teaching. Every year, in the month of Jyeshtha, many married Hindu women keep Vat Savitri. They fast, worship a banyan tree, wind thread around it, and tell this story aloud. In popular tellings Satyavan lay under a banyan, a tree that lives for centuries, so it stands for the long life Savitri won. A vrat like this is one of Hinduism's oldest ways to love someone: you give something up yourself, often food, and offer it for another person's long life. Savitri began with a three-night fast before her husband's last day, and finished with her words on the road.
screen: `A CONVERSATION WON, NOT A TRAP.` · `LET SATYAVAN LIVE.` · `VAT SAVITRI, UNDER THE BANYAN.` · then, large: `A VRAT FOR ANOTHER'S LONG LIFE.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind someone whose long life you wish for, someone you can still call or sit beside, and let their face come clear. Breathe in and notice that they're here; breathe out and wish them years. If you pray, offer a short prayer for their long life, the way women do on Vat Savitri; if not, simply hold the wish. If someone you've lost comes to mind instead, hold them kindly too.
Vara, a boon, the gift Yama kept offering Savitri on the road. A wife who talked with Death until he gave her husband back, and a vow women still keep under the banyan. Today's word.
Your line: a vrat offers your fast for another's long life. She carried the axe, and he leaned on her. Eight hundred days now.

screen: `DAY 800 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: THE DEER AND THE FIRE-STICKS.`

howItsDone: Markandeya ends the story by turning back to Yudhishthira's question about Draupadi. Outside the epic, many married women keep Vat Savitri in Jyeshtha: a fast, worship of a banyan, thread wound round it, and the story told aloud.

sources.ref: Mahabharata, Vana Parva, Pativrata-mahatmya Parva (Markandeya's story of Savitri): the fourth boon; Savitri's last speech; Satyavan restored; the walk home; Dyumatsena's sight; Markandeya's conclusion about Draupadi

notes: All paraphrase. Confirm in Ganguli the sequence: boon of sons for Savitri by Satyavan granted; a further speech; Yama asks her to choose an incomparable boon; she asks for Satyavan's life, saying she desires neither happiness, heaven, prosperity nor life without him.
Ganguli gives the number of sons and the length of the life Yama grants; omitted under the claims rule.
'Some retellings make this a clever trap' is a soft claim about popular tellings; a Keeper may prefer to cut it.
Confirm the walk home details: she binds her hair, carries the axe, supports him; the hermits reassure Dyumatsena; his sight is restored before they arrive.
The restoration of Dyumatsena's kingdom happens the next morning in the epic and is not narrated here.
Confirm that Yudhishthira's question to Markandeya concerned a woman as devoted as Draupadi, and Markandeya's closing line that Draupadi will save them.
